### `Y1` — HELD

**Measured.** pairs_carry_in_0: 531441; sum_wrong: 0; carry_wrong: 0; seconds: 1170; pairs_carry_in_plus_1_sampled: 4489; pairs_carry_in_minus_1_sampled: 4489; sampled_wrong: 0; sampling_stride: 11

**Note.** The carry-out was part of the claim on purpose. Without it the circuit is a mod-729 unit rather than an adder, and a sweep that ignored it would pass on a circuit that silently discards overflow.

### `Y2` — HELD

**Claim.** every pair settles in exactly seven passes, never six, whatever the carry does

**Measured.** pairs: 531441; not_exactly_seven: 0; passes_with_carry_crossing_all_six: 7; passes_with_no_carry: 7

**Note.** Derived before the run rather than probed: reachability is transitive closure, so a fully determined chain of switches resolves in ONE pass however long it is, and staging happens only where a gate is still unknown. Cell 0 resolves on pass 1, cell i on pass i+1, and pass 7 observes nothing changed. Ripple delay is invisible to a model with no delays in it -- the single cost a ripple adder is famous for is the one this model cannot show. Five hand-picked pairs had been checked during design; 531,441 is what made it a result.

**Note.** Registered as the most likely of the five to fail. A shared leaf ties two mid-level selectors to one node, so the shared circuit contains conducting paths BETWEEN mid nodes that the tree structure did not have -- identical tables do not in general imply identical circuits, and a pass network is where that distinction bites. Here they did.

### `Z1` — HELD

**Claim.** the free mid rail is load-bearing for exactly one published result, and it is the one that favoured ternary

**Measured.** w3_ternary_switches: 48; w3_binary_switches: 60; w3_ratio: 0.8; w3_mid_taps: 6; generator_switches_for_parity: 12; per_tap: 2; generator_switches_for_reversal: 13; adder_ternary_switches: 624; adder_binary_switches: 280; adder_parity_at: 0; adder_reversible: false

**Note.** T5 says the generator cannot be built inside the model at all: a divider between vss and vdd is two rails reaching one node, which is contention. So this break-even is a charge from outside the vocabulary rather than a circuit that could be drawn here. What can be said exactly is how dear it would have to be, and twelve switches is not dear.

### `Z2` — FAILED

**Claim.** buffering cannot take ternary pass depth below 4, and binary gets 3 for free

**Measured.** ternary_depths: {"none":6,"mid":4,"leafmid":4}; binary_depths: {"none":3,"mid":2,"leafmid":2}; ternary_floor: 4; binary_floor: 2; binary_unrestored: 3; decoded_cell_switches: 90; decoded_cell_depth: 3; selector_tree_cell_switches: 104; selector_tree_cell_depth: 6

**Note.** FAILED on its conclusion, not its numbers. The buffered floors are exactly as registered: 6 -> 4 -> 4 ternary and 3 -> 2 -> 2 binary. What failed is the clause that followed -- that 4 is the best depth ternary can buy AT ANY PRICE. Nothing measured quantified over designs; it quantified over where buffers go inside one family of selector trees. Decode the select instead of gating on it: a four-switch detector pulls to vss for LOW and HIGH and passes vmid for MID, paid once per select signal rather than once per selector, and then every selector arm is a single device including the middle one. The decoded adder cell reaches depth 3 -- equal to binary unrestored -- at 90 switches against 104, so it is shallower AND cheaper than the design the floors were measured on. Third time a clause in this repository outran its measurement; P3 and X2 were the others. Kept as FAILED, and the refutation is checked in test/test-midrail.js.

### `E4` — FAILED

**Claim.** exactly 13 passes for every operand pair, still independent of the data

**Measured.** predicted_passes: 13; observed_range: [9,13]; pairs_total: 531441; fraction: 128/243; selector_tree_passes: 7; selector_tree_varies: false; carry_table_leaves_with_low_and_mid_equal: 6; sum_table_leaves_with_low_and_mid_equal: 0; pairs_fewer_than_13: 279936; pairs_exactly_13: 251505; pairs_more_than_13: 0; buckets_sum_to_total: true

**Note.** FAILED on universality, not on arithmetic. Thirteen is correct as the WORST case, which is what the derivation actually bounded; the range is 9 to 13 and it DEPENDS ON THE OPERANDS. First circuit in the repository whose settling time is arithmetic rather than structural, and it scoped Y2 and Z5. Their independence-of-data result is a property of gating every arm on the RAW select, which makes all conduction known at one instant so nothing can settle early. Decoding splits the gating across two dependency levels: with the carry-in LOW the LOW arm already conducts while the MID arm gate is still unknown, so if both arms lead to the same rail the node is determined a pass early, by N3. Six of the carry table nine leaves have their LOW and MID cells equal; none of the sum table do. The three outcomes were separated on a second run: 279,936 settle in fewer than thirteen, 251,505 in exactly thirteen, and 0 in more. So 128 of every 243 settle early, and thirteen is a genuine ceiling rather than merely the predicted number. The count is no longer unexplained: the F set derives it exactly. The six agreeing carry leaves enable the saving, and the sum tree never being early is what decides which positions can use it.

The decoded design taps vmid 186 times against 168 -- one more per detector, eighteen of them -- because each detector reaches vmid through its own series pair. So the design that wins on switch count does it partly by leaning harder on the rail Z1 established that nobody is charging for. ### `F2` — HELD

**Claim.** the sum tree can never settle early, and that asymmetry is the whole result

**Measured.** combinations: 18; sum_tree_agreements: 0; carry_tree_agreements: 12

**Note.** Early settling needs the arm conducting on the raw select and the arm still waiting on the MID detector to lead to the same rail. For the carry tree that is carry(s+c) == carry(s), true for 12 of 18, because the carry function is flat over stretches. For the sum tree it is lowTrit(s+c) == lowTrit(s), true for none of them, because adding one always moves a low trit. So only the carry tree is ever early; the top position SUM is always the last node to move; and a saving at the top position is therefore invisible. That is exactly why the earlier naive count over-predicted by one, always in the same direction.

## Set `G` — Whether 251,505 appearing twice, from unrelated constructions, is anything

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 4 held, 0 failed |
| tool | `tools/collision-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-collision.js` |
| registered | `43c29b8` |
| results | `cd581ef` |

### `G1` — HELD

**Claim.** the correspondence dies at the first other parameter, and not narrowly

**Measured.** pairing: monoid width w against an adder of 3w trits; width_1_monoid_universe: 27; width_1_reach_any_carry: 27; width_1_reach_one_translation: 27; adder_3_trit_pairs: 729; adder_3_trit_late: 621; width_2_all_four: [531441,251505,531441,251505]

**Note.** Decisive in the bluntest available way. At width 1 the monoid acts on three points, so the entire space of functions there is 3^3 = 27 and every monoid at that width, whatever its vocabulary, is at most that. Both vocabularies do reach 27 -- at a single position the positionwise maps already give every unary function. The three-trit adder has 729 operand pairs of which 621 settle late. The monoid universe is smaller than the number it would have to match, so the failure is not a wrong value but no room for one.

### `G2` — HELD

**Claim.** and the two families grow at incompatible rates, so they were never one sequence

**Measured.** recurrence: s(k+1) = 9 s(k) - 12 s(k-1); holds_widths: 2..12; dominant_root: 7.372281; root_exact: (9 + sqrt 33) / 2; last_measured_ratio: 7.372282; monoid_growth_width_1_to_2: 9315; factor_apart: 1264; adder_counts_equalling_any_recorded_monoid_reach: [251505]

**Note.** The recurrence was derived by hand from the transfer matrix characteristic polynomial before the run and reproduces every count to width 12. Its dominant root is irrational, so the adder family multiplies by about 7.37 per step; the monoid multiplies by about 9,315 across the only span where both are computable. Across eleven adder counts and every monoid reach in the manifest, exactly one value coincides -- the one already known.

### `G3` — HELD

**Claim.** the collision is where two exponent sequences cross, once, not a pattern

**Measured.** monoid_ceiling_width_1: 27; monoid_ceiling_width_2: 531441; adder_pairs_3_trits: 729; adder_pairs_6_trits: 531441; as_powers_of_three: {"monoid":["3^3","3^12"],"adder":["3^6","3^12"]}

**Note.** They differ at the first width and agree at the second. No formula is claimed for how the monoid ceiling grows -- two data points do not determine one, and the question did not need it.

### `G4` — HELD

**Claim.** and collisions of this size are rare here, which is why one looked like something

**Measured.** integers_over_1000_in_two_or_more_sets: 4; crossing_the_two_halves: 2; crossing_values: [251505,531441]; restatements_within_one_half: [279936,4489]; halves_derived_from: which library each tool imports: monoid-lib or device.js; self_reference_excluded: the censusing set, matched by its tool name

**Note.** The instrument produced a false verdict first, and this is the fourth time that has happened here. The registration said prediction sets THAT MEASURE DIFFERENT THINGS and the first loop dropped the clause, counting 279,936 as colliding with itself because two sets record the same adder count, and 4,489 likewise because two sets share a sampling stride. Corrected by classifying each set by which library its tool imports -- derived, not hardcoded -- and requiring a collision to cross that line. The disambiguation rule was chosen after the first run, which is a degree of freedom worth declaring; it implements a clause that was in the registration beforehand, and the two excluded values are restatements of one quantity under any reading. Then a second correction, and a better one. Recording this very result put 279,936 and 4,489 into the manifest again -- as the values G4 had just EXCLUDED -- and on the next run they crossed the halves and G4 failed. The measurement had become part of the corpus it measures. A census cannot count the set that is the census; the tool and the test now drop it by matching the censusing tool name rather than an id.

### `H1` — FAILED

**Claim.** the solver is linear in devices times passes, not superlinear as the design documents assert

**Measured.** devices_swept: [8,64,512,4096,16384,50000]; predicted_spread_under: 3; measured_spread: [3.72,2.89]; predicted_exponent_band: [1,1.2]; measured_exponent: [0.917,0.931]; exponent_above_512_devices: 1.088; spread_above_512_devices: 1.64

**Note.** FAILED on both registered criteria, and the direction of the failure is the useful part. The exponent came in BELOW 1.0 both times - sublinear, better than predicted - because fixed per-solve overhead dominates the smallest networks and the derivation had no term for it. Above 512 devices, where overhead washes out, the spread is 1.64x and the exponent 1.088: both inside the registered band. Worse, the spread criterion was not reproducible - 3.72 on one run and 2.89 on the next, either side of the line it had been given. A criterion whose verdict depends on run-to-run noise is a defect in the prediction. The claim being tested is nonetheless settled: the solver is not superlinear, and the two documents saying so were corrected. The registration also mis-cited one of those documents as design/04-device-model.md, which is design/04-storage.md; the claim lives in design/10-integration.md, design/11-open.md and two doctree pillars, all four now corrected.

### `H2` — HELD

**Note.** The registered output was the crossover, and it is the sharpest thing this set produced: a full 531,441-pair sweep fits inside an hour only up to about 4,800 devices. The six-trit adder is 624 and sits comfortably inside. The machine is ~50,000 and does not. So the machine can be RUN and cannot be SWEPT, which makes it the first subject in this repository that sits outside the exhaustive discipline every other result rests on - and the exhaustibility precondition in METHOD.md stops applying to the thing the method was built to study.

### `H3` — HELD

**Claim.** charge retention changes nothing in the existing corpus

**Measured.** gate_node_values_compared: 210; gate_differences: 0; adder_node_values_compared: 221728; adder_differences: 0; patch: one rule: an isolated node keeps its previous value instead of becoming Z

**Note.** Zero differences anywhere. Derived before the run and confirmed: every circuit here is solved from a cold all-Z start, and a node with no previous value is Z under either rule. The two semantics can only diverge where a node is driven on one pass and isolated on a later one, which no existing circuit does. The comparison is not vacuous - test-headroom.js shows the two solvers DO differ on a written-then-isolated node, which is the case storage needs.

**Measured.** dynamic_cell_switches: 1; loop_breaking_cell_switches: 19; writes_all_three_trits: true; holds_all_three_across_a_seeded_solve: true; memory_729_words_retained: 4374; memory_729_words_loop_breaking: 48114; ratio: 11; design_phase_estimate: 5

**Note.** A single pass gate onto an isolated node writes and holds all three trits. One switch against nineteen, and the 729-word memory drops from 48,114 switches to 4,374 - eleven times, against the five the design phase estimated. Since memory is about 93% of the machine, this is the whole decision, and it costs nothing in the existing corpus by H3. The design documents ranking this change fourth by blast radius and first by leverage were right about the ordering and understated the size.

A computed DATA source is still rail-driven through whatever produced it, so it resolves rather than poisoning. What bites is an unresolved CONTROL node, which is unknown at pass one and gates rather than feeds. **Claim.** and I2 has two failure modes I0 cannot have

**Measured.** one_enable: {"bus":5,"correct":true}; two_enables: {"bus":["X","X","X",0,0,0],"sources":[5,-5]}; no_enable: {"bus":"all Z","consequence":"poisons any destination reading it (N6)"}; exclusion: {"I0":"structural -- every leg gated by the SAME select trit, and one trit cannot be LOW and HIGH at once","I2":"an invariant -- S separate enables must be one-hot, and something must uphold that every step"}

**Note.** Produced rather than asserted. And the two-enable result carries something nobody predicted: the bus goes X only on the trits where the two sources DISAGREE. 5 and -5 are trit-wise negatives, so they differ on three positions and agree (at zero) on the other three -- and the bus is X on exactly those three. A double-enable fault is therefore INVISIBLE whenever the contending sources happen to hold the same value. N4 does not say "contention is detected"; it says contention is X, and X only appears where there was something to disagree about. One correction to this audit's own first phrasing: it said "I0 has no shared node to contend for", which is false -- a tmux output IS shared between its legs. The difference is not whether a node is shared but how exclusion is guaranteed: I0 gates every leg on one select trit, so exclusion is structural; I2 needs S separate enables to be one-hot, which is an invariant something has to maintain. The comfortable phrasing was the wrong one.

### `A4` — HELD

**Claim.** and the decision does not belong to this phase

**Measured.** ledger: {"I0":{"precondition":"none - selects are inputs","failure_modes":"none","cost":"D x S"},"I2":{"precondition":"a second control cone, solved and seeded every step","failure_modes":"X on double-enable, Z on no-enable","cost":"S"}}; pick: PROPOSED, pending sequencing

**Note.** SCOPE COMMITMENT, NOT A FALSIFIABLE CLAIM ABOUT THE CIRCUIT. Recorded as HELD because the phase did what it registered it would do, but flagged so it does not become a template for padding sets with unfalsifiable process entries. It is the only prediction in twenty-one sets that is about the PHASE rather than the SUBJECT. I2 is 3.8x cheaper and needs a second control cone solved and seeded every step. Whether that is affordable is a question about how a step works, and design/09 is unbuilt -- so forcing the pick here would be deciding a sequencing question inside a wiring phase. Registered in advance that deferring is the expected outcome, so that it reads as a result rather than an omission. One bound the ledger needs: its I0 row says "no cold-start precondition -- selects are inputs", which is true of the RIG and not of the machine. In the assembled machine I0 selects come from instruction DECODE, which is a computed control node, so I0 inherits a control cone there too. The real comparison is therefore ONE cone (decode, already required by any design) against TWO (decode plus bus enables) -- which sharpens the deferral rather than weakening it.

## Set `D` — Which self-referencing ternary maps mix at all? A hashing question, answered by exhaustion at 729 states

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 2 held, 2 failed |
| tool | `tools/iterhash-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-iterhash.js` |
| registered | `cf1e0f8` |
| results | `d7e493b` |

### `D1` — HELD

**Claim.** a non-bijective f bleeds state and a permutation does not

**Measured.** random_map_image: {"after_1":461,"after_2":336,"after_5":200,"after_10":116,"after_20":56}; predicted_after_1: 461; formula: N(1 - 1/e) = 461; predicted_below_200_by_step_10: true; random_permutation_image_after_20: 729

**Note.** Exact. So the structural rule holds and is now measured rather than asserted: an iterated hash of this shape must use a PERMUTATION, and its compression must come from TRUNCATION at the end. A non-bijective f throws away a third of the space on the first call.

### `D2` — HELD

**Claim.** any positionwise f has period at most 6, at every width

**Measured.** maps_checked: 36; largest_order: 6; every_order_divides_6: true; widths: holds at any width by the lcm argument

**Note.** The whole positionwise family is dead for this purpose, provably rather than statistically. A trit permutation has order 1, 2 or 3; applying one per position, f^m is the identity exactly when every position is, so the order is an lcm drawn from {1,2,3}. A state of ANY width returns to itself within six calls. This is strictly stronger than Q4's 27^w ceiling, because a ceiling still permits a large orbit and a period of six does not.

### `D3` — FAILED

**Claim.** cross-trit coupling breaks the period bound and rotate(s + sbox(s)) resembles a random permutation

**Measured.** f_pos: {"order":3,"cycles":243}; f_rot: {"order":6,"cycles":130}; f_add: {"order":2,"cycles":365}; f_addrot: {"order":6,"cycles":130}; random_permutation_baseline: {"cycles":6.6,"fixed":1}; predicted_f_addrot_within_factor_2_of: 6.6; first_run_registered_candidate: {"sbox":"contained the NEGATION permutation","f_add_image":16,"f_addrot_image":16,"note":"the registered candidate's actual first result, before the s-box was corrected"}

**Note.** Wrong, and wrong twice over. First the sub-claim that s + sbox(s) is not in general a permutation held, but for a reason worth more than the claim: it is injective exactly when the s-box is an ORTHOMORPHISM (see F-ORTHOMORPHISM-GATE). Second, and the actual failure: with a correct orthomorphic s-box, rotate(s + sbox(s)) still lands at 130 cycles against a baseline of 6.6. It does not resemble a random permutation at all. The reason the prediction missed is that a positionwise 3-cycle IS addition of a constant, so s + sbox(s) stays AFFINE, and affine maps over this ring have tiny order. Fixing the s-box fixes injectivity and does nothing whatsoever for mixing. Carry alone is not enough; the addend must be nonlinear in s.

### `D4` — FAILED

**Claim.** truncated collisions separate a mixing f from a positionwise one

**Measured.** f_pos: 0.96x expected; f_rot: 0.96x expected; f_addrot: 0.96x expected; empty_buckets: 0/27 for all; predicted_f_pos: far off, too few collisions

**Note.** All three land at 0.96x, indistinguishable from each other and near-ideal -- including the positionwise map that D2 proves repeats every six calls. The prediction missed because truncating ANY permutation to three trits yields exactly 27 buckets of 27, which is perfectly uniform by construction. So uniformity is what a permutation gives away for free, and a collision count CANNOT distinguish a good hash from a relabelling. This failure is worth more than the prediction would have been: it disqualifies the most obvious test anyone would reach for.

## Set `M` — Reversible universality: ternary reaches it at two operands, binary provably cannot

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 4 held, 0 failed |
| tool | `tools/reversible-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-reversible.js` |
| registered | `8ce0662` |
| results | `ac0d590` |

### `M0` — HELD

**Claim.** the Schreier-Sims instrument reproduces four known group orders exactly, in BigInt

**Measured.** 27-cycle: 27; S_27: 27! = 10888869450418352160768000000; A_27: 27!/2 = 5444434725209176080384000000; AGL(3,3): 303264; cross_check: the M3 group enumerated by brute force (151,632 elements) matches the chain exactly

**Note.** Four of five on the first run, and the fifth was the TEST CASE rather than the tool: it paired a 3-cycle with a 25-CYCLE, which between them move only 25 of the 27 points, and the tool correctly returned 25!/2 -- the right answer to the question actually asked. Scored WRONG against an expectation of 27!/2. A test case that does not generate what its name says is an instrument-false-verdict aimed at the instrument instead of at itself. Both cases are now kept, the 27-point one and the 25-point one, with their correct expectations.

### `M1` — HELD

**Claim.** binary has no non-affine two-bit reversible gate and ternary has 362,448

**Measured.** binary: {"states":4,"all_reversible":24,"affine":24,"non_affine":0,"affine_share":"100.000%"}; ternary: {"states":9,"all_reversible":362880,"affine":432,"non_affine":362448,"affine_share":"0.119%"}; closure_verified_by: membership, x -> Ax + b, on every element of the generated group

**Note.** Exact, no sampling. Reversible 2-bit gates are 4! = 24 and |AGL(2,2)| = 6 x 4 = 24, so every one of them is affine. Reversible 2-trit gates are 9! = 362,880 and |AGL(2,3)| = 48 x 9 = 432. Since affine maps compose to affine, an all-affine gate set generates a subgroup of AGL however it is wired -- so binary two-bit gate sets cannot reach the symmetric group at ANY width, which is why binary reversible computation needs a three-bit gate.

### `M2` — HELD

**Claim.** a named width-two ternary gate set generates exactly A_27, as its parity forces

**Measured.** generators: ["INC(t0)","C1INC(t0,t1)","C1INC(t1,t2)","C1INC(t2,t0)"]; parities: all even; non_affine_generators: 3 of 4; order: 5444434725209176080384000000; equals: A_27 exactly; family_sample: 20 of 20 random non-affine 2-trit gates reach at least A_27, against a predicted 15 of 20

**Note.** Predicted from parity rather than left to chance: INC is nine disjoint 3-cycles and each C1INC is three, a 3-cycle is even, so the group lies inside the alternating group and S_27 was forbidden before the run. It came out exactly A_27. C1INC is non-affine because the indicator of t == 1 is quadratic over GF(3). The family half was registered separately so one gate would not be read as the family, and 20 of 20 cleared the bar.

### `M3` — HELD

**Claim.** the same wiring with an affine gate stays inside AGL(3,3)

**Measured.** order: 151632; agl_3_3: 303264; index_in_agl: 2; fraction_of_symmetric_group: 1.39e-23; elements_enumerated: 151632; elements_failing_membership: 0

**Note.** One gate changed from non-affine to affine -- same widths, same wiring, same four generators -- and universality disappears by twenty-three orders of magnitude. Checked by MEMBERSHIP and not by an order bound: all 151,632 elements were enumerated and every one is of the form x -> Ax + b. An order bound would have passed for any small group. The group is index 2 in AGL(3,3) because all four generators are even.

**Note.** Exhaustive over one variable in both fields. This is set M's advantage traced to its root: the simplest possible conditional -- act if the control equals a specific value -- is LINEAR in binary and NONLINEAR in ternary, so binary must AND two controls together to get nonlinearity and that is why it needs a three-bit gate. Restricted to ONE control digit on purpose: the indicator of a single POINT of two binary digits is quadratic too, which is what x AND y is, so the general claim would be false.

So an outer trigger is five times cheaper per gate, not twice. Caveat as registered: this is the per-gate marginal cost, and E/I showed a MID detector amortises across every selector sharing a control, so in a machine it may be a wash.

**Note.** Both derived numbers hit exactly, and both gates verified correct exhaustively. Built in the SAME pass-network idiom with T5 obeyed on both sides -- every source rail-driven, buffers counted, no trick used on one side and withheld from the other. An earlier estimate put the binary side at ~22 by building it from NAND gates while giving the ternary side pass-transistor tricks; that strawman is recorded rather than quietly dropped. Two operands instead of three buys 1.2x, not 3x.

### `O4` — HELD

**Measured.** at_price_0: {"ternary":10,"binary":12,"winner":"ternary"}; at_price_1: {"ternary":12,"binary":12,"winner":"tie"}; at_price_2: {"ternary":14,"binary":12,"winner":"binary"}; at_price_4: {"ternary":18,"binary":12,"winner":"binary"}

**Note.** The tie lands at exactly the predicted price. The device model's FIRST stated limit is that vmid is free and it calls that the largest of the four; the ternary gate takes two mid taps and the binary gate takes none. So the honest statement is not "ternary is cheaper" -- it is that ternary's advantage is STRUCTURAL and not economic, and every switch of the economic margin is borrowed from the one assumption this model flags as its biggest. A myth killed before it was built on.

## Set `T` — The control word, and whether instruction decode can be made to disappear

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 3 held, 1 failed |
| tool | `tools/decode-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-decode.js` |
| registered | `d951dc7` |
| results | `c4be374` |

### `T1` — HELD

**Claim.** the control word is sufficient: an opcode-blind interpreter reproduces src/vm.js exactly

**Measured.** programs: 8; agreed: 8; steps_compared: 566; compared_on: A, C, PC, output length, halted, every step

**Note.** The ground truth the rest of the set rests on. The interpreter takes the opcode only to look up its control word and then never refers to it again -- every branch is driven by a control field. If the table were missing a distinction, some program would diverge. None does. Note that this establishes SUFFICIENCY, not that the table is a good design: a table can be sufficient and still be poorly factored.

### `T2` — HELD

**Claim.** and it is eleven trits wide, injective, and too wide to fit the opcode cell

**Measured.** field_widths: {"op":1,"rd":1,"wr":1,"ix":1,"alu":3,"dst":1,"pc":1,"io":2}; total_trits: 11; distinct_control_words: 25; opcodes: 25; injective: true; opcode_trits_needed: 3; cell_trits: 6; spare: 3; fits: false

**Note.** Exactly as derived. The control word is injective, so it carries precisely the opcode information -- spread across eleven trits instead of three. And eleven does not fit in six, so the FREE version of C5 is dead: decode cannot be made to vanish by widening the opcode into the spare trits of its own cell. That is the headline, and it is a fact about this control table rather than about ternary.

### `T3` — HELD

**Claim.** and no field can be direct-encoded into a three-trit opcode

**Measured.** rule: a field of width w fits iff max class <= 3^(3-w); class_sizes: {"op":[16,5,4],"rd":[14,11],"wr":[23,2],"ix":[23,2],"alu":[7,6,2],"dst":[16,7,2],"pc":[22,2,1],"io":[22,1,1,1]}; verdicts: 16>9, 14>9, 23>9, 23>9, 7>1, 16>9, 22>9, 22>3 -- none fits; any_fits: false

**Note.** Every registered class size matched. Registering them exactly is what made a miscount catchable, and it caught one during the derivation: an earlier version of the fit rule asked only "max class <= 9", which is correct for a ONE-trit field, and reported the three-trit ALU field as fitting on a max class of 7. The cap for width w is 3^(3-w), which for that field is 1. Caught before the registration was written rather than after.

### `T4` — FAILED

**Claim.** the best jointly direct-encodable subset totals 6 trits and is jointly injective

**Measured.** best_subset: ["op","rd","alu"]; best_width: 5; max_joint_class: 3; jointly_injective: false; predicted_width: 6; predicted_injective: true; trits_freed: 5 of 11; decode_outputs_remaining: 6; saving: 45%; decode_full: 572 switches; decode_after: 312 switches

**Note.** Wrong by exactly one trit, and wrong about injectivity. Six trits of spare capacity exist, but NO subset of fields totalling six is jointly injective on the 25 opcodes -- the fields are chunky (widths 1,1,1,1,3,1,1,2) and no combination summing to six separates every opcode. The best is five trits, with a max joint class of 3 that the one remaining trit exactly covers. So the saving is 45% of decode rather than the 55% predicted, still at zero memory cost because the spare trits were already paid for. The prediction being optimistic by one trit is the whole error.

**Claim.** and seeding it makes it settle to a fixed point, which is the problem

**Measured.** seeded_then_resolved: 3; froze: 2; advanced: 0; failed_to_resolve: 1

**Note.** Nothing advanced. Seed the control cone the way the memory array in C had to be seeded and the handshake resolves -- to ONE state, which a second solve does not move. So the seeding is not a workaround for the handshake: the SEEDING IS THE CLOCK, and it is external. That is the concession arriving from a different direction.

### `AA3` — HELD

**Claim.** so the concession is forced by the model, not chosen by the design

**Measured.** solver_outputs_checked: 45; genuine_fixed_points: 45; states_that_moved_on_a_second_solve: 0

**Note.** Every state the solver returns is a genuine fixed point: re-solving from it with the same inputs returns it unchanged, across every circuit family checked. So the solver contract is that it returns a state where nothing changed, or it throws. A sequencer needs SUCCESSIVE DISTINCT states, so sequencing inside one solve would require a network that does not settle -- and not settling is an error rather than an output. Q3 is unavailable in principle here rather than merely difficult, and the concession in design/09 is a consequence of the model rather than a weakness of the design.

## Set `AB` — Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 3 held, 2 failed |
| tool | `tools/erasure-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-erasure.js` |
| registered | `152a70c` |
| results | `06fefa1` |

### `AB1` — HELD

**Claim.** information-preserving two-input operations are rare in ternary, and much rarer than in binary

**Measured.** ternary_reversible_tables: 216; ternary_tables_total: 19683; ternary_fraction: 1.097%; binary_reversible_tables: 4; binary_tables_total: 16; binary_fraction: 25.0%; ratio_of_fractions: 22.8; affine_over_GF3: 18; non_affine: 198; column_criterion_vs_full_pair_sweep: 100/100 agree

**Note.** Predicted 216, 4, 18 and 198 exactly, and every one landed. The instruction map is (A,W) -> (f(A,W), W), injective exactly when each of the three columns of the table is a bijection of the three trit values -- 6^3 = 216. Binary has 2 columns and 2 permutations each, so 4 of 16. The argument was not trusted: the column criterion was checked against a direct sweep of all 531,441 pairs on a sample of tables, and agrees on every one. The gap is the point -- a randomly chosen two-input ternary operation is about 23 times less likely to be reversible than a binary one, which is the same asymmetry M1 found on the 27-point arena arriving on the 729-point one.

### `AB2` — HELD

**Claim.** the erasing instructions are not the ones that overwrite the accumulator

**Measured.** preserving: 11; erasing_fixed: 4; erasing_operand_dependent: 5; families_or_three_place: 5; STORE_bits_erased: 9.5098; STORE_writes_accumulator: false; LOAD_bits_erased: 9.5098; ADD_bits_erased: 0

**Note.** Scored against the CLAUSE language, and the registration was ambiguous about which reading it meant -- worth stating rather than leaving for a checker to find. The header said "under the datapath state", and this tool defines that as the (accumulator, addressed word) PAIR for an address operand; under that strict reading MIN, MAX and CSUM are single fixed figures, the split is 7 fixed and 2 varying, and AB2 fails. But the clauses say "for every operand" and "depends on the operand", which only parse if the operand is a parameter rather than part of the state -- and the operand-dependence clause is not even well-formed under the pair reading. Scored on the clauses, every predicted count and every predicted membership held. The tool prints both readings side by side so neither is hidden. The load-bearing part held too: STORE erases the full 9.5098 bits and never touches the accumulator. Under the pair state it maps (A,W) to (A,A), destroying the addressed word outright -- the textbook Landauer erasure sitting in plain sight in an instruction set nobody wrote for thermodynamics, and the instruction whose name says it is SAVING something. ADD by contrast is a permutation of the entire 531,441-pair datapath, because the operand survives in memory: it is exactly the difference between ADD and K.

### `AB3` — HELD

**Claim.** erasure is data-dependent, exactly as settling time turned out to be in E4

**Measured.** MIN_min_bits: 0; MIN_max_bits: 9.5098; MIN_mean_bits: 4.5033; MIN_at_all_plus_one: 0; MIN_at_all_minus_one: 9.5098; MAX_mirrors_MIN: true; CSUM_min_bits: 0; CSUM_max_bits: 4; CSUM_mean_bits: 2.6667; SHL_equals_SHR_for_every_n: true; shift_bits_per_trit: 1.5849625

**Note.** The mean 4.5033 was derived before the run as 6*(0 + 2/3 + log2 3)/3 and measured at 4.5033. CSUM was predicted never to reach the maximum and does not -- it tops out at exactly 4 bits, so a single tritwise gate cannot erase a whole tryte however hostile its operand. SHL n and SHR n erase identically at n*log2 3: one drops the high trits and one the low, and an information count cannot tell those apart, which is a real limit of this measure and not a fact about the machine.

### `AB4` — FAILED

**Claim.** and therefore the charge is not recoverable from the program text, which is precisely the property the static count has and this does not

**Measured.** programs: 8; programs_priced: 8; programs_where_text_bound_exceeds_actual: 2; programs_where_text_bound_is_exact: 6; largest_overcharge: 1.21; predicted_largest_overcharge: > 2

**Note.** FAILED, and the failure is the answer to the question the set was opened to ask. Predicted a gap for every program and a factor above two for at least one; measured a gap for two of eight and a largest factor of 1.21. Six of the eight programs charge EXACTLY their text bound, because every opcode they execute is fixed-price -- the operand-dependent instructions (MIN, MAX, CSUM, SHL, SHR) simply do not appear in them. So the static count DOES transfer, conditionally: erasure is recoverable from the program text exactly when the instruction mix is operand-independent, and this repository's programs mostly are. The tick's virtue is not lost here, it is contingent on the ISA subset in use, which is a sharper claim than either the prediction or its negation.

### `AB5` — FAILED

**Claim.** the machine erases by convention, not by necessity: the named zero-erasure ALU generates 1,458, and admitting the reversible tables lifts it to the full symmetric group

**Measured.** named_ALU_group_order_at_width_6: 1458; named_ALU_closed_form: 2 * 3^W; reversible_fragment_width_1: 6; reversible_fragment_width_2: 324; reversible_fragment_width_3: 12754584; reversible_fragment_width_4: 194522647344910860816; reversible_fragment_width_5: 172512988791785396199665263632922083814221660243633706214496; reversible_fragment_closed_form: 2^W * 3^((3^W - 1)/2); closed_form_matches_at_widths: 1 through 5; symmetric_group_reached: only at width 1; width_6_extrapolated_digits: 176; symmetric_group_729_digits: 1773

**Note.** The first clause HELD exactly: 1,458, which is the 729 translations extended by negation, verified by sifting all 1,459 instruction maps through a chain built from two of them. The second clause FAILED, and inverts the conclusion. Admitting every one of AB1's 216 reversible tables at every operand does NOT reach the symmetric group. The orders land on a closed form, 2^W * 3^((3^W-1)/2), matching exactly at widths 1 through 5. Width 1 is the only place reversibility is free -- there the fragment IS S_3. From width 2 the fraction collapses: 324 of 362,880, then 10^-21, then 10^-100. So REVERSIBILITY DOES NOT BUY UNIVERSALITY here, and the eraser is load-bearing rather than a convention of the opcode table -- the same shape as the result that no term over {B,C,W,I} can select. Registered honestly: at width 6 the stabiliser chain had not finished after two hours on this host, so 2^6 * 3^364 is the closed form extrapolated from five exactly measured widths, NOT a measurement. "Does not finish" would be a duration claim, which is T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE and the class this project has already bitten twice; what is recorded is what was observed.

## Set `AC` — Can a program's cost be learned without paying it? The implied-receipt question

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 1 held, 3 failed |
| tool | `tools/predict-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-predict.js` |
| registered | `e5ffa3f` |
| results | `acebf26` |

### `AC1` — FAILED

**Claim.** only two of the eight programs have an input-dependent step count, and they are countdown and fold

**Measured.** programs: 8; predicted_varying: 2; actual_varying: 3; varying: countdown, multiply, threeway; fold_varies: false; programs_executing_IN: 8; predicted_executing_IN: 5; read_input_but_cost_a_constant: 5

**Note.** Failed on the count, on the membership, and on its own premise. fold does NOT vary; multiply and threeway do. And the premise that five of eight execute IN was itself wrong -- ALL EIGHT do, which a broken detector had hidden. The corrected picture is sharper than the prediction and points the same way the design question cares about: reading input is universal here and cost-invariance is still the norm. FIVE OF EIGHT PROGRAMS COST EXACTLY THE SAME NUMBER OF STEPS whatever data they are handed, so their price can be published once and nobody ever needs to run them again. multiply varies only mildly, 119 to 128, because its loop is bounded by trit count rather than by operand size; the variation is in the early-exit paths, not the iteration count.

### `AC2` — HELD

**Claim.** where the cost does vary it is cheaply predictable: countdown is exactly affine in its input, fitted from two runs and exact on the rest

**Measured.** fitted_from: N=1 (8 steps) and N=2 (13 steps); model: steps = 5*N + 3; inputs_checked: 200; exact_predictions: 200; worst_error: 0; cost_of_the_predictor: 2 executions

**Note.** Exact on 200 of 200, worst error zero. Two executions price two hundred, and the ratio only improves with the size of the sweep. This is the cheapest possible refutation of an implied receipt for this program: the number can be had without doing the work, so holding the number proves nothing about work performed. Data-dependence alone establishes NOTHING -- it is necessary for an implied receipt and nowhere near sufficient.

### `AC3` — FAILED

**Claim.** two programs exist with identical instruction count and identical opcode histogram whose step counts differ by more than 100x, and the achievable ratio exceeds 300x

**Measured.** ratio: 182.5; cheap_program_steps: 4; dear_program_steps: 730; predicted_over: 300; exceeds_100x: true; identical_instruction_count: true; identical_opcode_histogram_naive_reader: true; identical_opcode_histogram_real_tokenizer: true; differing_source_lines: 1

**Note.** The structural claim HELD and the number FAILED. Two programs differing in a single immediate operand -- LOADI 1 against LOADI 364 -- have the same instruction count and the same opcode histogram under both a naive linear reader and the assembler's own tokenizer, and cost 4 steps against 730. Any predictor reading only the static shape of a program returns one number for both and is wrong on one by a factor of 183. That is a counterexample rather than a failed search, and it settles the question against SYMBOL COUNTING specifically: a price computed from a program's text cannot track what running it costs. The 300x figure was optimistic for a reason worth recording -- the four-step floor of the cheap program sits in the denominator, so the ratio is 730/4 and not 364/1. Predicting a ratio without accounting for constant overhead is the same error as quoting a speedup without the serial fraction.

### `AC4` — FAILED

**Claim.** bits erased per executed instruction varies across the eight programs by more than 2x, and the program with the most steps is not the one with the highest erasure per step

**Measured.** spread: 1.68; predicted_spread_over: 2; highest: fold.tasm at 6.0757 bits per step; lowest: tgate.tasm at 3.6228 bits per step; most_steps: interp-core.tasm; most_bits_per_step: fold.tasm; same_program: false

**Note.** Failed on the number, held on the ordering. The spread is 1.68x against a predicted 2x, which is narrower than expected -- the eight programs are more alike in erasure intensity than in anything else this project has measured about them, all falling between 3.6 and 6.1 bits per instruction. But the ordering claim held: the program that runs the longest is not the one that destroys the most per step. So a currency denominated in steps and one denominated in destroyed information do rank these programs differently, just less dramatically than predicted. Choosing between them remains a decision rather than a units conversion, on a narrower margin than the prediction assumed.

## Set `AD` — A loop bound the program discovers, and whether that is enough for an implied receipt

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 4 held, 0 failed |
| tool | `tools/hailstone-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-hailstone.js` |
| registered | `8175f9b` |
| results | `bc9efb5` |

### `AD1` — HELD

**Claim.** the two-point fit that priced countdown exactly fails here, and the cost is not monotone in the input

**Measured.** terminating_inputs: 363; total_inputs: 729; fitted_model: steps = 2*N - 2, from N=1 (0 steps) and N=2 (2 steps); exact_predictions: 2; exact_percent: 0.6; countdown_exact_percent: 100; monotonicity_inversions: 33; adjacent_pairs: 242; lengths_min: 0; lengths_max: 19; distinct_lengths: 20

**Note.** The same procedure that priced countdown on 200 of 200 inputs is right on 2 of 363 here -- 0.6% against 100%. And the cost is not monotone: 33 of 242 adjacent pairs run the wrong way as the input grows, which rules out any predictor built from the magnitude of the input alone. So a DISCOVERED loop bound really is a different object from a READ one, and hailstone is the first program in this repository that has one.

### `AD2` — HELD

**Claim.** a patient predictor still wins: the full cost table costs at most 729 map evaluations, re-running costs more than 3,000, and the crossover is under 100 queries

**Measured.** memoised_tabulation_evaluations: 728; predicted_at_most: 729; naive_rerun_evaluations: 3777; predicted_over: 3000; mean_cost_per_query: 10.4; crossover_queries: 70; predicted_crossover_under: 100; table_agrees_with_runner: true

**Note.** Every one of the 729 accumulator values is resolved exactly once -- 728 evaluations, one short of the state count because the terminating value is seeded. Answering the same questions by independent re-running costs 3,777. So a predictor expecting more than SEVENTY queries should tabulate, and from the seventy-first onward every answer is free. Being genuinely discovered is therefore NOT SUFFICIENT for an implied receipt. The predictor does not have to be clever; it is allowed to be patient.

### `AD3` — HELD

**Claim.** no single-accumulator trajectory can exceed the state space, for this map or any other, and the observed maximum sits far below the ceiling

**Measured.** longest_trajectory: 19; state_space: 729; headroom_used_percent: 2.61; terminating_trajectories_revisiting_a_value: 0

**Note.** Demonstrated rather than asserted: every terminating trajectory was checked for a revisit and none has one, so each is a simple path through the state space and cannot exceed 729 steps. The bound is pigeonhole and belongs to the state space rather than to hailstone -- it holds for any single-accumulator map whatever. The observed maximum uses 2.61% of the available headroom, so the tabulator wins by a wide margin rather than a narrow one.

### `AD4` — HELD

**Claim.** the cost depends only on the accumulator, so the tabulation bound is tight, and the security parameter is reachable state count rather than loop shape

**Measured.** inputs_unchanged_under_poisoned_scratch: 729; inputs_whose_cost_changed: 0; states_at_0_extra_words: 729; states_at_1_extra_word: 531441; states_at_2_extra_words: 387420489; states_at_3_extra_words: 282429536481

**Note.** Every scratch word was poisoned before the run and all 729 answers were unchanged, so the cost really is a function of the accumulator alone and AD2's bound of 729 is tight rather than generous. The arithmetic that follows is DERIVED: each live word beyond the accumulator multiplies the tabulator's one-off cost by 729 while leaving the runner's single query untouched. Taken with AD2 this is the result of the set -- THE SECURITY PARAMETER OF AN IMPLIED RECEIPT IS REACHABLE STATE COUNT, not whether the loop bound is discovered. That is the same shape as key length, and a different design problem from the one the question started with.

## Measured but never registered

Facts established in passing. Listed separately so the pre-registration record is
not inflated by things that were never at risk.

- **`F-ADD-IS-A-TABLE`** — ADD equals TOPC with the 27-row addition table, exactly.
  <br>*Evidence:* checked over every operand pair
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-fold.js`
- **`F-ORDER-K-MASKING`** — An interpreter bug that permutes the emulated semantics has an ORDER, and is invisible at layer counts divisible by it. Order 2 is masked at 2 layers; order 3 at 3.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-selfhost.js`
- **`F-FOLD-BUYS-DEPTH`** — Folding buys a level of emulation depth, not just instructions: the unfolded chain is refused at depth 4 and the folded one runs.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-fold.js`
- **`F-TGATE-NOT-CLOSED`** — TGATE's three modes are not closed under composition: 6 of its 8 two-stage composites are not any TGATE mode. This is why TOP folds and TGATE cannot.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-fold.js`
- **`F-KLEENE`** — Reading -1/0/+1 as false/unknown/true, MIN, MAX and NEG are exactly the connectives of Kleene's strong three-valued logic. Excluded middle and non-contradiction both fail at unknown.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-logic.js`
- **`F-RADIX-ECONOMY`** — Base 3 is the cheapest integer radix by the radix-economy measure: representing a million values costs 40 in base 2, 39 in base 3, 40 in base 4.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-logic.js`
- **`F-BRANCH-BENEFIT`** — Three-way dispatch beats two-way on the same machine by about half an instruction and a fifth of the code per decision point, and nothing at all when the decision is genuinely binary. Deep dispatch loses outright to an indexed jump: 149 cells against 30.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-bench.js`
- **`F-531441-COINCIDENCE`** — The top rung of the ladder is 531,441, numerically identical to the source conversation's figure, by coincidence. That figure counted two-stage configurations of 6-trit trytes (729^2); this counts elements of a monoid on 9 points (9^6). Both are 3^12 for unrelated reasons, and the conversation's claim about what it counted remains wrong.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-monoid.js`
- **`F-GATES-FROM-SWITCHES`** — The standard ternary inverter computes NEG on all three inputs; MIN and MAX are correct on all nine rows. Switch counts: STI 4, NTI 2, PTI 2, MIN 8, MAX 8.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-device.js`
- **`F-FOUR-SWITCH-NEG-NOT-UNIQUE`** — The standard ternary inverter is not the only four-switch NEG in this model. Exhaustive search finds four distinct networks, and it is one of them.
  <br>*Evidence:* 148,995 four-switch networks over 42 device types, all solved
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-axioms.js`
- **`F-SUM-LEAVES-COLLAPSE`** — The sum tree of a balanced-ternary full adder has only three distinct leaf selectors of nine, and the carry tree five, because both depend on a+b rather than on a and b separately.
  <br>*Evidence:* hash-consing the leaf selectors takes the six-trit adder from 624 switches to 384
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-adder.js`
- **`F-INPUTS-DO-NOT-SOURCE`** — An input gates a device and terminates a path, but never sources one: a conducting device between an input and a node transfers nothing, and the node is Z. Reachability starts at rails and only at rails.
  <br>*Evidence:* proved as the second half of T5; no circuit in the repository had ever used an input as a pass terminal, so nothing had depended on it either way
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-axioms.js`
- **`F-251505-AGAIN`** — The number of operand pairs on which the decoded adder settles in exactly thirteen passes is 251,505 â€” the same figure the monoid audits found for what positionwise logic plus one carrying ADD reaches at width two. Two different objects counted inside the same 3^12 space, landing on the same six-digit number.
  <br>*Evidence:* 531,441 minus the 279,936 that settle in fewer passes; the rung is recorded in the U set
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-decoded.js`
- **`F-WRAP-VERSUS-STEP`** — The sum and carry halves of a balanced-ternary adder save in exactly complementary currencies, and for one reason. The low trit WRAPS, so its rows repeat across operand sums -- nine leaf selectors collapse to three -- but its cells never agree within a row, so it can never settle early. The carry STEPS, so its rows never repeat -- five of nine, no collapse -- but it is flat over stretches, so twelve of eighteen cells agree within a row and it settles early constantly.
  <br>*Evidence:* sum tree 3 distinct rows and 0 of 18 in-row agreements; carry tree 5 distinct rows and 12 of 18
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-passcount.js`
- **`F-TREE-DEPTH-SPLIT`** — The tmux/dmux split measured on one selector holds on a 27-way three-level read tree over stored cells: tmux reads all 27 addresses, dmux reads only the 9 whose every address trit is MID and never settles on the other 18.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/terminal-audit.js, naive seeding, all 27 addresses, both families
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-terminal.js`
- **`F-CONTENTION-IS-DATA-DEPENDENT`** — Bus contention resolves to X only on the trits where the contending sources differ, so a double-enable fault is completely invisible when they hold equal values.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/interconnect-audit.js, two enables asserted with sources holding 5 and -5: X on the three trits where they differ, 0 on the three where both are zero
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-interconnect.js`
- **`F-ORTHOMORPHISM-GATE`** — For a positionwise g, the map s -> s + g(s) is injective exactly when g is an orthomorphism, i.e. when t -> t + g(t) is itself a permutation of the trits. Exactly 3 of the 6 trit permutations qualify -- the identity and the two 3-CYCLES -- and all three involutions fail. Negation is the worst possible choice: s + (-s) = 0 collapses all 729 states to one.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/iterhash-audit.js, all 6 trit permutations, exhaustive over 729 states; the orthomorphism test predicts the image size exactly (729 or collapsed) in every case
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-iterhash.js`
- **`F-SPLIT-ROUND-MIXES`** — Splitting the state and using one half to modify the other is invertible for ANY round function. With a NONLINEAR 27-entry round table, across 20 different tables, the cycle count runs 2..12 with mean 6.8 against ln(729)=6.6 and 19 of 20 inside two standard deviations -- consistent with a random permutation. The same structure with a LINEAR round function gives 92 cycles and order 8, so the structure is not what mixes: the round function's nonlinearity is.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/iterhash-audit.js, exhaustive over 729 states, 20 shuffled round tables plus a linear-round control
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-iterhash.js`
- **`F-UNIFORMITY-IS-NOT-MIXING`** — Truncating any permutation to m trits gives perfectly uniform buckets by construction, so a truncated-collision count cannot distinguish a mixing function from a relabelling. A map proved to repeat every six calls scores 0.96x the random-function expectation, the same as every other permutation tested.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/iterhash-audit.js, D4: three structurally different permutations all score 0.96x with 0 empty buckets
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-iterhash.js`
- **`F-ALWAYS-ONE-FIXED-POINT`** — The split-state construction has EXACTLY ONE fixed point for every round table -- 1 in all 20 sampled, never 0 and never 2 -- where a random permutation gives Poisson(1) and would have none about 37% of the time. The state with L = R and round(R) = 0 is fixed; the round table is a permutation, so exactly one R maps to 0. That is a structural fingerprint rather than a statistic, and a fixed point is an input that no number of rounds ever moves. The standard remedy is a per-round CONSTANT, which collides with the one-function-called-repeatedly rule unless the round counter is carried inside the state.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/iterhash-audit.js, 20 shuffled round tables, exhaustive over 729 states; the fixed state is -336, where L=R=1 and round(1)=0
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-iterhash.js`
- **`F-BORN-NONLINEAR`** — The design intuition inverts between the two bases. In binary, linear operations are cheap and nonlinearity is something you construct by combining controls; in ternary, the simplest one-control conditional is ALREADY nonlinear and linearity is the special case you have to work to obtain -- t_b += t_a is affine and needs deliberate choosing, while "if t_a equals 1" is not and comes for free.
  <br>*Evidence:* O1 exhaustively over both fields at one variable; M1/M3 showing 0.119% of reversible 2-trit gates are affine against binary's 100%
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-nonlinearity.js`
- **`F-REVERSIBLE-FRAGMENT-CLOSED-FORM`** — The group generated on 3^W accumulator states by every information-preserving instruction -- translation, negation, and all 216 reversible tritwise tables at every operand -- has order exactly 2^W * 3^((3^W - 1)/2). Nobody predicted a closed form; it was read off a ladder of exactly computed orders and then checked against every width the chain could reach.
  <br>*Evidence:* AB5, widths 1 through 5: 6, 324, 12754584, 194522647344910860816, and a 60-digit value, each matching the formula exactly
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-erasure.js`
- **`F-STATE-BOUNDARY-DECIDES-THE-READING`** — An instruction has two different and equally correct erasure figures depending on where the state boundary is drawn. MIN reads as a single fixed 4.5033 bits when the operand is folded into the state, and as a range from 0 to 9.5098 when the operand is a known parameter -- and the fixed figure is exactly the mean of the range. Neither reading is wrong; the boundary is a modelling choice that must be declared before any number means anything.
  <br>*Evidence:* AB2, both readings computed side by side for MIN, MAX and CSUM
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-erasure.js`
- **`F-COST-INVARIANCE-IS-THE-NORM`** — All eight programs in this repository execute IN, and five of them cost exactly the same number of steps regardless of what they are given. Cost-invariance is the norm here rather than the exception, which nobody predicted and which is the single most important fact for any scheme that wants a step count to be evidence of work performed.
  <br>*Evidence:* AC1, seven input vectors per program including the empty one and both tryte extremes
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-predict.js`
- **`F-TIMES-THREE-CANNOT-MIX`** — A hailstone rule of the form 3n + k cannot mix on a base-three machine. Multiplying by three always zeroes the low trit, so the low trit is k forever after the first climb: the value can never become divisible again and every trajectory runs to the fixed point of an affine map. Swept over all 729 inputs, 3n+1 terminates on exactly six of them -- the powers of three. Replacing the climb with 2n + low_trit mixes the residue and terminates on 363. Measured while choosing the rule, not predicted.
  <br>*Evidence:* AD, five candidate growth rules swept over all 729 inputs before the set was registered
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-hailstone.js`

## Defect classes

Each produced a wrong result that looked right. The count is how many times each
recurred, which is itself a measure of how well naming a thing prevents it.

| class | times | shape |
|---|---|---|
| `T-ONE-POINT` | 3 | Comparing two functions at a single input and concluding they are equal. Bit the mixed-TGATE test, the folded-vs-unfolded programs, and the TOP-vs-ADD comparison, where 81 of 19,683 tables matched at one pair. |
| `T-STALE-CONSTANT` | 4 | A hardcoded count in a test or a document going stale when the thing it counted grew. The closure test kept passing against an opcode list the source no longer had; test-findings.js miscounted its own prediction sets; and the README stated both a check total and a prediction tally that had drifted. The first two were fixed by deriving them. The third could not be owned by any one suite, because it is the sum of all of them, so run-all.js sums the suites and test-findings.js recomputes the tally. Fifth bite: the decode audit hardcoded the direct-encodable width as 6 in its cost section, two lines below the search that had just measured it as 5 -- so it printed a saving the measurement immediately above it had already refuted. The cost section now reads the search result. A constant is not safe merely because the thing it duplicates is nearby. |
| `T-SILENT-NAN` | 1 | Writing through a missing label produced an undefined address, so the write silently did nothing. The core interpreter ran with no control register and no complaint. |
| `T-ADJACENCY` | 1 | .fold reading nine cells from a table that was shorter, silently borrowing whatever followed it. |
| `T-EXHAUSTED-NOT-CLOSED` | 3 | Confusing ran out of budget with finished. A search that exhausts its depth limit, one that hits its size cap, and one that genuinely closes are three different outcomes; conflating them produced a false negative verdict on V3. It recurred in the E sweep, where one counter held both settled-sooner-than-predicted and needed-longer-than-predicted, and the correctness check was skipped for the second bucket -- so an exhaustive claim was published while resting on an unmeasured decomposition. That time the numbers happened to be right: the second bucket was empty. Report the outcomes separately and check that they sum to the total. Third bite, this time in a CHECKER rather than an instrument: the staged solver was compared against solve() by crediting agreement only when both settled, so the cases where both agreed precisely that the network does NOT settle were counted as disagreements, and the tool declared its own results suspect. |
| `T-SOURCE-NOT-TERMINAL` | 1 | Switch-level reachability traversing THROUGH a driven node. A path from one rail that touches another rail and continues out of it makes correct circuits look contended. Rails and inputs are ideal sources and must terminate a path. |
| `T-INSTRUMENT-FALSE-VERDICT` | 14 | The measuring tool, not the thing measured, producing the failure. V3 read depth exhaustion as saturation; W2 traversed reachability through rails; X5 keyed a network by ordered terminals when D4 says terminals have no order; G4 dropped a qualifier that was present in its own registration and counted a quantity restated in a second set as colliding with itself. Each reported a verdict about the world that was a fact about the instrument. When a result contradicts a prediction, suspect the instrument first, and check the loop against the sentence that was registered. Fourth bite: the terminal audit held its storage cells with hold=LOW, which is the WRITE configuration -- the hold switches are n-types at threshold HIGH, so LOW opens the feedback loop and every cell floats. Every one of 81 cases in both families read Z, and the audit would have reported the roadmap blocking question as answered NO. A verdict of "nothing works" against a family that demonstrably works is the instrument. Fifth bite: the memory rig built its decoder with the first address trit MOST significant and its read tree with that trit LEAST significant. Each half was internally consistent; together they addressed different words for 18 of 27 addresses, so writes appeared to land in the wrong place and every read-back failed. Two halves of one address path disagreeing about endianness reads exactly like a broken circuit. Sixth bite: the interconnect rig named its sources `src0_0`, `src1_0`, ... and SEEDED them, without building anything behind them. A seed is an initial value, not a driver -- T5 says reachability starts at rails and only at rails -- so every source resolved to Z on pass one and stayed there. Both topologies routed Z, which read as "interconnect does not work at all" rather than "these are not sources". The same fact this repository already records as "an input gates but never sources", arriving in a form nobody recognised. Seventh bite, and inverted: a TEST CASE accused a correct instrument. The Schreier-Sims verification paired a 3-cycle with a 25-cycle and called the pair "A_27"; between them they move 25 of 27 points, so the tool returned 25!/2 -- exactly right for what was actually built -- and was scored WRONG. When a verification case fails, the case is as suspect as the thing it checks. Eighth bite: the sequencer rig called tAdderCell without its TAG, which names every internal node of the cells two tables. All three cells received the tag `undefined`, so their internal trees shared node names and merged into one circuit -- the incrementer resolved to unknown and the sequencer appeared to visit two states instead of twenty-seven. An omitted parameter that looks optional silently welded three circuits together. Ninth bite, in the same phase and pointing the other way: the handshake section counted the two driving values that DISABLE the loop as "settled cleanly", which would have reported a self-timed handshake as working on the strength of two circuits in which no handshake occurs. A false positive and a false negative from one tool in one run. Two more, found by reconciling this list against results/07-negative.md, which had one occurrence the manifest never named and lacked two the manifest did: the detector truth table hand-copied from a comment and INVERTED, which produced 36 failures out of 54 -- every one where the middle word disagreed with the selected word and none where they agreed, the exact signature real contention would leave, reading as the publishable headline that the decoded selector cannot read storage. Two views of one list drifted apart in opposite directions, which is what a second copy of a record is for and against. Twelfth bite: AB2s first erasure census folded the operand INTO the state, which is a defensible boundary and not the one AB2 asked about, so MIN read as a single fixed 4.5033 bits when the registered prediction was about a range from 0 to 9.5098 -- a correct computation about a different question, which would have recorded a prediction as FAILED when it held in full. Thirteenth bite, and it produced the most interesting wrong headline yet. AC1 detected whether a program reads input with a regex anchored at the start of the line, which misses every LABELLED instruction -- threeway.tasm carries "body: IN". So the audit reported a program that never reads input whose step count nonetheless varied with the input: a deterministic machine charging different amounts for data it never touches, which would have been the finding of the set. It was a broken parser standing next to an exported real one. Replaced with the assembler's own tokenizer, which moved the count of input-reading programs from five to eight and changed what AC1 was even about. Fourteenth bite, and it pointed the flattering way, which is the dangerous one. AD2's tabulator memoised only TERMINATING values, so each of the 366 divergent inputs walked its full three-thousand-step guard, learned nothing, and left the next divergent input to do it again: 1,098,362 evaluations to price 729 inputs. It reported a patient predictor as three hundred times WORSE than simply re-running, which is exactly the answer that would have made AD2 fail and the implied receipt look sound. Non-termination is an answer too, and a correct tabulator records it; walking until the path meets either a known value or itself resolves every state once and costs 728. An instrument that errs toward the hypothesis under test will not be caught by finding the result surprising, because it is not surprising. |
| `T-PREMISE-NOT-ANSWER` | 1 | A prediction failing on an assumption it never stated rather than on the quantity it asked about. X2 asked which seeds are self-consistent and assumed every seed resolves; two do not. The assumption, not the answer, was the falsifiable part. |
| `T-FAKE-RANDOM` | 1 | A sampling instrument that was not sampling. A seeded generator multiplied a 31-bit seed by a 31-bit constant, which overflows the 53 bits a JS number holds exactly, so the low-order bits it returned were rounding noise: three of its eight node names were drawn essentially never and no random network ever floated or contended. It looked like 400 trials and was closer to 400 repetitions of one. Random input needs a vacuity check on what it actually produced, not on how many times it ran. |
| `T-CHECK-FORBIDS-HEALTHY-STATE` | 2 | A consistency check that treated a legitimate intermediate state as a defect. It demanded that tools/ and the manifest prediction sets be equal in number; they are equal only between phases, because registering a tool predictions and recording its results are deliberately separate commits. During a registration there is one more tool than there are sets, and that is the protocol working. The check now names the pending tool instead of failing on it. Second bite: the design-folder status-marker check scanned for bare vocabulary words with a word boundary, and a new trap id -- T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE -- contains UNKNOWN between hyphens. The check failed a document whose vocabulary was entirely correct, because an identifier is not a marker. |
| `T-SEARCH-WHERE-A-CHECK-WOULD-DO` | 1 | An instrument that searched for a value it could have verified. Finding the exact pass count by scanning k = 1 upward cost up to eighty solves per input on a 1,776-switch network and did not finish inside ten minutes. The count is the same for every input, so it needs finding once and checking twice thereafter -- settles at k, does not settle at k-1. Two solves, not eighty. |
| `T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN` | 2 | A measured result stated as a property of the SUBJECT when it was a property of the DESIGN measured. Z2 swept buffer placements in one family of trees and concluded a depth floor for ternary at any price; a different selector beat it. E4, and Y2 and Z5 before it, measured raw-select circuits and concluded settling time is never data-dependent; a decoded selector made it data-dependent. Both times the numbers were right and the noun was too big. Before writing ternary, or this model, ask whether the sweep visited more than one design. |
| `T-CENSUS-COUNTS-ITSELF` | 1 | A measurement over a corpus that the measurement is then written into. G4 surveyed the manifest for repeated integers, and recording its own result added those integers to the manifest a second time -- as the values it had excluded -- so the next run found them colliding and the prediction failed against its own record. Nothing was wrong with the world or the first answer. If a result is stored where it will later be read as data, exclude the storing record from the read, and derive the exclusion from something structural rather than an id. |
| `T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE` | 2 | A registered criterion whose verdict depends on run-to-run variation. H1 predicted a spread under 3x and measured 3.72 on one run and 2.89 on the next, either side of its own line, so the same world produced both a pass and a fail. The attempt to salvage a more robust shape from it flipped too. A threshold placed near the noise floor is a defect in the prediction rather than a fact about the subject; either widen it until it cannot flip, or measure the quantity and report it without asserting a bound. Second bite, and it was sitting inside the suite that records the first. test-headroom section 5 checked "the six-trit adder is sweepable inside an hour" against a LIVE timing. It passed on an idle machine and failed at 1.84 h inside a full suite run on a loaded one -- the same world returning both verdicts. Section 4 of the same file already refuses to assert durations and enforces that refusal by grepping itself; section 5 was quietly doing what section 4 forbids, four sections below the comment explaining why not to. The repair is the one the class prescribes: assert the RATIO, which survives any host -- a 50,000-device sweep costs about 80x a 624-device one -- and report the hour figures without checking them. On the loaded host the measured sweep budget is 335 devices against H2 recorded 4,806, so the figure was never a constant of nature and is now labelled as a measurement taken on a stated machine. |
| `T-TRANSCRIBED-TABLE` | 1 | A fact that could have been RUN was hand-copied instead. The terminal audit seeded a detector output from its truth table as written in a comment. The comment was right; the transcription inverted it, putting an n-type gate above its threshold so a selector leg conducted on exactly the addresses where it must be off. The result was not noise: 36 of 54 cases failed, every one of them a case where the middle word disagreed with the selected word and none where they agreed -- the exact mechanistic signature real contention would produce, and a plausible headline finding. A wrong instrument does not look wrong. When a value is derivable by running a two-line network, run it rather than copying it. |
| `T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE` | 1 | A control signal that is a COMPUTED node rather than a primary input is unknown on the first pass of the fixed point, and unknown conduction is treated as possible -- so on pass one it bridges or breaks everything it gates. Counted ONCE, not twice: B1a predicted exactly this shape for a decoded selector's middle leg in its own registration commit BEFORE the run, which is the protocol working rather than a trap anyone fell into. It bit in C, where nothing in the registration anticipated it: every hold gate in a 27-word array is a decoder output, and all 26 unaddressed words went to X on every write. The cells hold perfectly when hold is a primary input and not at all when it is a decoder output. The fix is not a workaround -- solve the control cone on its own and seed it. The general shape is that a circuit correct at its fixed point can be unreachable from a cold start, and the larger the control fan-out the more it takes with it. |
| `T-SCOPE-DECIDES-THE-VERDICT` | 3 | A correct computation scored a prediction wrongly because the measurement drew its state boundary somewhere the prediction did not. N1 asked whether a BUILD puts MID on a node when the registered rule was whether the FUNCTION requires it, and scored the detector FORCED while the next section built the same function with zero taps. AB2's first census folded the operand into the state, which is a defensible boundary and not the one AB2 asked about, so MIN came out as a single fixed figure while the clauses spoke of a range, and AB2 would have been recorded as FAILED. Both readings are defensible and the registration did not say which it meant, so the honest diagnosis is an ambiguous registration as much as a mis-scoped instrument. The defence is to state the boundary in the registration and to report every reading the question admits rather than one. Third bite, and this one arrived from a LATER set rather than from the instrument itself. G4 censuses the manifest for integers appearing in both the vocabulary half and the circuit half; its classifier returns a third value, other, for a tool requiring neither, and the crossing test counted other as a side. Set AB then recorded 19,683 -- the size of the two-input tritwise function space, which Q also holds -- and a set belonging to NEITHER half read as crossing between them. The computation was correct and the question was not the registered one. Scoped to the two named halves, which is a structural exclusion rather than an id. |
| `T-TOOL-CHECKED-ONLY-BY-IMPORT` | 1 | A tool that is exercised only through require(), so the path it takes when actually RUN is never covered. The erasure audit was made silent on import by a mechanical rename of every console.log call to log -- which rewrote the body of log itself into a call to itself. The tool crashed with a stack overflow on every single run, and every check in its suite stayed green, because a test that imports the module sets MAIN false and no print path ever executes. Nothing about the numbers was wrong; the program was simply broken in the half nobody looked at. The antibody is a check that spawns the tool as a subprocess and asserts it exits cleanly and printed every section, made affordable by an environment variable that caps its most expensive sweep. Mutation-tested: reintroducing the recursive definition turns all three of those checks red. |
